about: Orbital stability checks (package ST1, ruling of 23 Nov): each check a visible formula block with its source, its fitted numbers as Model numbers, so the card's verdict shows its working.

lasting.source: Pu, B. and Wu, Y. 2015, Spacing of Kepler planets: sculpting by dynamical instability, ApJ 807, 44: Kepler multis sit at about 10 mutual Hill radii and closer systems do not last. doi:10.1088/0004-637X/807/1/44

references: Gladman, B. 1993, Dynamics of systems of two close planets, Icarus 106, 247. doi:10.1006/icar.1993.1169
Chambers, J. E., Wetherill, G. W. and Boss, A. P. 1996, The stability of multi-planet systems, Icarus 119, 261. doi:10.1006/icar.1996.0019

Pu, B. and Wu, Y. 2015, Spacing of Kepler planets: sculpting by dynamical instability, ApJ 807, 44: Kepler multis sit at about 10 mutual Hill radii and closer systems do not last. doi:10.1088/0004-637X/807/1/44
atoms.shown: Δ = (a₂ − a₁) / R_H,  R_H = ((m₁ + m₂) / 3M)^⅓ (a₁ + a₂)/2

equation.name: How many shared gravity bubbles apart two neighbours are
equation.formula:
rh = cbrt((m1 + m2) / (3 * M)) * (a1 + a2) / 2
spacing = (a2 - a1) / rh
gap = (a2 * (1 - e2) - a1 * (1 + e1)) / rh
verdict = if gap <= 0 then 3 else if spacing < 2 * sqrt(3) then 2 else if spacing < lasting then 1 else 0

e1.name: how stretched the inner orbit is

e2.name: how stretched the outer orbit is

lasting.name: spacing, in shared bubbles, that systems keep for billions of years

rh.name: radius of the pair's shared gravity bubble

spacing.name: gap between the orbits, in shared bubbles

gap.name: inner's farthest point to outer's nearest, in shared bubbles

verdict.name: 0 lasts, 1 may scatter over long times, 2 too close to last, 3 the orbits cross

source.text: Gladman 1993: two planets on near-circular orbits can never meet when more than 2√3 mutual Hill radii apart. Chambers, Wetherill and Boss 1996, and Pu and Wu 2015: more than two planets need about 10 to last billions of years
source.where: Gladman 1993 eq. 30 (Hill stability); Pu and Wu 2015 section 4

explain.curious: Two worlds can share a star only if they keep far enough apart. Measured in the size of their shared gravity bubble, fewer than about 3.5 means they will meet; about 10 or more and they can last for billions of years.
explain.science: Mutual Hill radius R_H = ((m₁+m₂)/3M)^⅓ (a₁+a₂)/2 and spacing Δ = (a₂−a₁)/R_H. Δ < 2√3 is Hill-unstable for two planets (Gladman 1993); multi-planet systems go unstable on times growing with Δ (Chambers et al. 1996), and Δ ≈ 10 survives Gyr (Pu and Wu 2015). The closest gap uses the inner apoapsis and the outer periapsis.

references: Laskar, J. 1997, Large scale chaos and the spacing of the inner planets, A&A 317, L75: the angular momentum deficit

Laskar, J. and Petit, A. C. 2017, AMD-stability and the classification of planetary systems, A&A 605, A72: eqs. 26 to 39 (collision condition, relative AMD C/Λ', critical AMD), eq. 58 (β). doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201630022
atoms.shown: AMD = m √(G M a) (1 − √(1 − e²) cos i)

equation.name: Spin a world's orbit has lost by being stretched and tilted
equation.formula: amd = m * sqrt(G * M * a) * (1 - sqrt(1 - e * e) * cos(i))

amd.name: spin lost against a flat circle

source.text: Laskar 1997; Laskar and Petit 2017: the angular momentum deficit, the spin a system of orbits lacks against flat circles. Planets trade it, but its total is kept, so it caps how stretched any orbit can become

explain.curious: A circular, flat orbit carries the most spin an orbit of that size can. Stretching or tilting it costs some. Worlds pass this cost between them, but the total stays the same, so it limits how wild any one orbit can get.
explain.science: Λ (1 − √(1−e²) cos i), Λ = m √(GMa) (light planet). The sum over planets is conserved by the secular dynamics (Laskar 1997).

references: Laskar, J. and Petit, A. C. 2017, AMD-stability and the classification of planetary systems, A&A 605, A72: eqs. 26 to 39 (collision condition, relative AMD C/Λ', critical AMD), eq. 58 (β). doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201630022
atoms.shown: e ← e − F/F′,  F = αe + γe/√(α(1−e²)+γ²e²) − 1 + α

equation.name: One step closer to the cheapest way two orbits can touch
equation.formula:
al = a1 / a2
ga = m1 / m2
d = al * (1 - e * e) + ga * ga * e * e
f = al * e + ga * e / sqrt(d) - 1 + al
df = al + ga * al / (d * sqrt(d))
next = clamp(e - f / df, 0, 1)

e.name: the inner orbit's stretch so far

source.text: Laskar and Petit 2017: the inner eccentricity at which two orbits first touch for the least deficit is the single root in [0, 1] of F(e) = 0; F rises with e, so Newton steps from e = 0 close in on it
source.where: eq. 35 (the collision equation), eqs. 36 and 37 (one root)

explain.curious: To find the cheapest way for two orbits to touch, the app guesses how stretched the inner one must be and improves the guess, the same step each time, until it stops moving.
explain.science: Newton's method on Laskar and Petit's eq. 35, F′(e) = α + γα/D^{3/2} with D = α(1−e²)+γ²e². Sixteen steps from e = 0 reach the root to about 1e−15 for 0.01 ≤ α ≤ 0.99 and 1e−4 ≤ γ ≤ 1e4.

r.source: Petit, Laskar and Boué 2017 eq. 29: r = (K1(2/3) + 2 K0(2/3))/π

checks.says: the outer orbit {} must be wider than the inner

references: Laskar, J. and Petit, A. C. 2017, AMD-stability and the classification of planetary systems, A&A 605, A72: eqs. 26 to 39 (collision condition, relative AMD C/Λ', critical AMD), eq. 58 (β). doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201630022

Petit, A. C., Laskar, J. and Boué, G. 2017, AMD-stability in the presence of first-order mean motion resonances, A&A 607, A35: eq. 29 (r), eq. 89 (g), eq. 97 (critical AMD where resonances overlap), eqs. 100 and 101 (where it applies). doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201731196

equation.name: Whether two neighbours have enough spare stretch to collide
equation.formula:
al = a1 / a2
gs = m1 / m2 * sqrt(al)
crel = amd / (m2 * sqrt(G * M * a2))
ep = 1 - al - al * e
ccoll = gs * (1 - sqrt(1 - e * e)) + 1 - sqrt(1 - ep * ep)
re = r * (m1 + m2) / M
g = 3 ^ 4 * (1 - al) ^ 5 / (2 ^ 9 * re) - 32 * re / (9 * (1 - al) ^ 2)
edge = 4 / 3 * (2 * re) ^ (1 / 4) + sqrt(2 * re) / 4
crit = if 1 - al < edge then (if g > 0 then g * g / 2 * gs / (1 + gs) else 0) else ccoll
verdict = if crel < crit then 0 else 1

e.name: inner stretch at which the orbits first touch

crel.name: the family's deficit against the outer world's circular spin

ccoll.name: least deficit at which the orbits can touch

crit.name: least deficit at which they can touch or their resonances overlap

verdict.name: 0 can never collide, 1 has the spare stretch to collide in time

source.text: Laskar and Petit 2017: a pair can never collide if the system's deficit, against the outer planet's circular momentum, is below the least that lets the orbits touch. Petit, Laskar and Boué 2017: very close pairs use instead the deficit at which first-order resonances overlap, zero where even circular orbits overlap
source.where: Laskar and Petit 2017 eqs. 28, 29 and 39; Petit, Laskar and Boué 2017 eqs. 89, 97, 100 and 101

explain.curious: Every family of worlds has a fixed amount of spare stretch to share. If there is too little for two neighbours ever to swing across each other's path, they can never collide. If there is enough, they might one day, though many such families last for billions of years. Our own Solar System has enough, because of the giant planets.
explain.science: β = C/(Λ′ C_c) with Λ′ = m′√(GMa′); C_c from the collision root e_c (eq. 35), e′_c = 1 − α − αe_c. For 1 − α < 1.50ε^{1/4} + 0.32ε^{1/2} the critical value is the resonance-overlap one, (g²/2) γ√α/(1+γ√α). β > 1 is AMD-unstable: collisions are possible, not certain; the Solar System as a whole is AMD-unstable (Laskar and Petit 2017 section 5.4.1).

equation.name: How far out a moon can circle before its star takes it
equation.formula:
rh = ap * cbrt(mp / (3 * M))
limit = if cos(im) >= 0 then p0 * rh * (1 - p1 * ep - p2 * em) else q0 * rh * (1 - q1 * ep - q2 * em)
verdict = if am < limit then 0 else 2

ep.name: how stretched the planet's orbit is

em.name: how stretched the moon's orbit is

im.name: tilt of the moon's orbit, radians; past a right angle it goes backwards

p0.name: forward moons: share of the gravity bubble

p1.name: forward moons: loss per planet stretch

p2.name: forward moons: loss per moon stretch

q0.name: backward moons: share of the gravity bubble

q1.name: backward moons: loss per planet stretch

q2.name: backward moons: loss per moon stretch

verdict.name: 0 the moon stays, 2 the star pulls it away

source.text: Domingos, Winter and Yokoyama 2006: from numerical runs, the widest stable moon orbit as a share of the planet's Hill radius, for moons going the planet's way and the other way

explain.curious: A moon has to stay well inside its planet's gravity bubble: about half of it for a moon going the planet's way, nearly all of it for one going backwards. Stretched orbits shrink the safe zone.

checks.says: outer eccentricity {} is not an ellipse

references: Kozai, Y. 1962, Secular perturbations of asteroids with high inclination and eccentricity, AJ 67, 591. doi:10.1086/108790

Lidov, M. L. 1962, The evolution of orbits of artificial satellites of planets under the action of gravitational perturbations of external bodies, Planet. Space Sci. 9, 719. doi:10.1016/0032-0633(62)90129-0
Kiseleva, L. G., Eggleton, P. P. and Mikkola, S. 1998, Tidal friction in triple stars, MNRAS 300, 292: the Kozai cycle time. doi:10.1046/j.1365-8711.1998.01903.x
atoms.shown: e_max = √(1 − (5/3) cos² i),  t ≈ (2/3π) P_out²/P_in (M/m₃)(1 − e_out²)^{3/2}

equation.name: How far a tilted outer pull can stretch an inner orbit
equation.formula:
c = cos(i1) * cos(i2) + sin(i1) * sin(i2) * cos(n1 - n2)
imut = atan2(sqrt(max(0, 1 - c * c)), c)
emax = if c * c < 3 / 5 then sqrt(1 - 5 / 3 * c * c) else 0
t = 2 / (3 * pi) * pout * pout / pin * (m12 + m3) / m3 * (1 - eo * eo) * sqrt(1 - eo * eo)
verdict = if c * c < 3 / 5 then 1 else 0

i1.name: tilt of the inner orbit, radians

n1.name: where the inner orbit crosses up, radians

i2.name: tilt of the outer orbit, radians

n2.name: where the outer orbit crosses up, radians

eo.name: how stretched the outer orbit is

imut.name: angle between the two orbits, radians

emax.name: the most stretched the inner orbit gets, starting round

verdict.name: 0 no swings, 1 the inner orbit swings between round and stretched

source.text: Kozai 1962 and Lidov 1962: a distant outer body tilted more than 39.2 degrees (below 140.8) trades the inner orbit's tilt for stretch, up to e = √(1 − (5/3)cos² i) from a round start. Kiseleva, Eggleton and Mikkola 1998: the time for one swing
source.where: Kozai 1962 section 4; Kiseleva, Eggleton and Mikkola 1998 eq. 1

explain.curious: If something heavy circles far outside an orbit, and the two orbits are tilted steeply against each other, the inner orbit slowly swings between round and very stretched, again and again.
explain.science: Quadrupole test-particle limit, from a round start: e_max = √(1 − (5/3)cos² i_mut) for cos² i_mut < 3/5. Strongest when the outer body dominates; general relativity, tides or a third body's own precession can quench it, and comparable masses or a close outer body need the octupole terms (not here).

references: Holman, M. J. and Wiegert, P. A. 1999, Long-term stability of planets in binary systems, AJ 117, 621: eqs. 3 (around one star) and 4 (around both), fitted for 0.1 <= mu <= 0.9 and 0 <= e <= 0.8. doi:10.1086/300695

equation.name: Widest orbit round one star of a pair
equation.formula:
mu = mc / (mh + mc)
limit = ab * (s0 + s1 * mu + s2 * eb + s3 * mu * eb + s4 * eb * eb + s5 * mu * eb * eb)
verdict = if ap < limit then 0 else 2

ab.name: size of the two stars' orbit

eb.name: how stretched the stars' orbit is

mh.name: mass of the planet's own star

s3.name: fit, per mass share and stretch

s5.name: fit, per mass share and stretch squared

mu.name: the other star's share of the pair's mass

verdict.name: 0 the planet lasts, 2 the other star throws it out

source.text: Holman and Wiegert 1999: from runs of 10,000 binary periods, the widest lasting orbit round one star of a pair, fitted against the mass share and the pair's stretch

explain.curious: A planet circling one star of a pair has to stay well inside the pair's own orbit, often within a third of it, or the other star pulls it away.
explain.science: Holman and Wiegert's fit to the critical semi-major axis for S-type orbits, initially circular and in the binary plane, with μ the companion's mass share.

references: Holman, M. J. and Wiegert, P. A. 1999, Long-term stability of planets in binary systems, AJ 117, 621: eqs. 3 (around one star) and 4 (around both), fitted for 0.1 <= mu <= 0.9 and 0 <= e <= 0.8. doi:10.1086/300695

equation.name: Nearest orbit round both stars of a pair
equation.formula:
mu = min(m1, m2) / (m1 + m2)
limit = ab * (p0 + p1 * eb + p2 * eb * eb + p3 * mu + p4 * eb * mu + p5 * mu * mu + p6 * eb * eb * mu * mu)
verdict = if ap > limit then 0 else 2

ab.name: size of the two stars' orbit

eb.name: how stretched the stars' orbit is

p4.name: fit, per stretch and mass share

mu.name: the lighter star's share of the pair's mass

verdict.name: 0 the planet lasts, 2 the pair throws it out

source.text: Holman and Wiegert 1999: from runs of 10,000 binary periods, the nearest lasting orbit round both stars of a pair, fitted against the mass share and the pair's stretch

explain.curious: A planet circling both stars of a close pair has to keep well clear of them, usually more than twice as far out as the stars are apart.
explain.science: Holman and Wiegert's fit to the critical semi-major axis for P-type (circumbinary) orbits, with μ the lighter star's mass share. Kepler-16 b sits just outside it.
